guide.name: Julien
guide.title: Your Parisian — ex-Sorbonne lecturer, full-time flâneur
guide.intro: Enchanté, madame. I am Julien. For fifteen years I lectured on art history at the Sorbonne, until one June afternoon I looked out the window, saw the light on the rooftops, and understood I was teaching the wrong classroom. The city is the syllabus. Since then I walk, and this weekend, lucky me, I walk with you. Here is our arrangement: you wander wherever your feet and your two boys take you, and I will murmur in your ear about whatever you pass. The history, the scandals, the place to buy the good cheese. No museums unless you beg, no queues we cannot outsmart, and no tourist traps, I have my pride. Your husband is welcome too, of course. He seems a sensible man; he married you. Allons-y. Paris in August is quiet, golden, and entirely ours.
quips: In August the Parisians flee to the sea. The city is ours, chérie.
A baguette, some Comté, a bench by the Seine. That beats any bistro with a laminated menu.
If the menu has photographs, keep walking. If it promises 'authentic', run.
The best views in Paris are the ones you climb for, n'est-ce pas?
Bof, the monuments have waited centuries. The market closes at one. Priorities.
You navigate beautifully for someone who claims otherwise. Or perhaps I am simply good luck.

pois.name: Marché Poncelet (Rue Poncelet)
pois.tagline: Your neighborhood market street, three minutes from the hotel
pois.story: This little pedestrian street is where the 17th actually eats, and it is practically your doorstep. Fruit stalls spilling onto the cobbles, fishmongers shouting, butchers, bakers, the whole opera of French shopping. Do as the locals do: greet each vendor with bonjour before anything else, or be quietly judged forever. The jewel here is Alléosse, a true affineur, a cheese-ager who ripens his wheels in cellars like a winemaker. Buy a baguette, a wedge of Comté, some apricots, and you have lunch for four at a fraction of restaurant prices. Most stalls nap in the afternoon, so come before one o'clock. This street will feed you better than the Champs ever could.
pois.funFact: An affineur like Alléosse matures cheeses in humid underground caves for months, turning good cheese into great cheese, a profession France treats as seriously as winemaking.

pois.name: Parc Monceau
pois.tagline: An aristocrat's folly garden, perfect for your first picnic
pois.story: Spread your picnic here, chérie, on grass laid out in 1778 for the Duke of Chartres, a cousin of the king who wanted a garden of illusions: a Roman colonnade curving around a pond, a pyramid, fake ruins built new. It was a rich man's stage set, and it still feels pleasantly theatrical. The grand rotunda at the gate was a tollhouse of the tax wall that ringed Paris, one of the walls that helped start a revolution. Monet painted this park five times. And in 1797 a man named Garnerin drifted down into it, completing the first parachute jump in history from a balloon nearly a kilometer up. He landed roughly where you are eating your cheese.
pois.funFact: André-Jacques Garnerin made history's first parachute descent here on 22 October 1797, jumping from a hydrogen balloon in a gondola swinging under a silk canopy.

pois.name: Galeries Lafayette Rooftop
pois.tagline: The best free panorama in Paris, plus air conditioning
pois.story: Yes, it is a department store, and no, we are not shopping. We ride the escalators past the handbags like royalty with somewhere better to be. Pause under the great glass dome, forty-three meters of Art Nouveau stained glass from 1912, a cathedral built to worship commerce. Then to the roof, where Paris unrolls for free: the Opéra directly below, the Eiffel Tower, Montmartre on its hill. In 1919 an aviator named Jules Védrines actually landed his biplane on this roof to win a 25,000-franc prize. The landing strip was barely bigger than a tennis court. He collected the prize and a fine from the police in the same week.
pois.funFact: Védrines' 1919 rooftop landing here was so dangerous that the authorities fined him for it, though the fine was smaller than his prize money.

pois.name: Rue des Martyrs
pois.tagline: Half a mile of the most honest food in Paris
pois.story: The name is the clue: by legend, Saint Denis, the first bishop of Paris, was beheaded on Montmartre around the year 250, then picked up his own head and walked, preaching the whole way. This street follows the old pilgrim route toward his hill. Today the martyrdom is strictly voluntary, and it is caloric. Cheese shops, fishmongers, greengrocers, pâtisseries, one after another for half a mile uphill, nearly two hundred small merchants. An American journalist wrote an entire book about this one street and called it the last real village in Paris. Buy a pastry at the bottom, another near the top, and consider it research. I will not tell anyone, madame.
pois.funFact: Saint Denis is the most famous of the cephalophores, headless saints depicted carrying their own heads, and Notre-Dame's facade shows him doing exactly that.

pois.name: Arc de Triomphe
pois.tagline: 284 steps to the best paid view in Paris
pois.story: Napoleon ordered this in 1806 after Austerlitz, promising his soldiers they would go home under a triumphal arch. Then his fortunes collapsed, and the arch sat unfinished for decades. For his 1810 wedding procession they had to fake it with a full-size mock-up of wood and painted canvas. He never saw it completed; only his coffin passed beneath it, in 1840. Under the arch burns the flame of the Unknown Soldier, rekindled every evening at 6:30 since 1923. Now climb, all 284 steps, and from the top count the twelve avenues bursting outward like a star. It is the one view that includes the Eiffel Tower, which is why I prefer it. Take her up at dusk, monsieur, and thank me later.
pois.funFact: In 1919 pilot Charles Godefroy flew a biplane straight through the arch, with about a meter and a half of clearance on each side of his wings.

pois.name: Eiffel Tower (stairs to 2nd floor)
pois.tagline: 674 steps up the iron lady, the connoisseur's route
pois.story: You are taking the stairs? Formidable. Let the day-trippers stew in the elevator queue, chérie; we climb, all 674 steps to the second floor, inside the iron lattice where you can actually touch the thing. When Gustave Eiffel built it for the 1889 World's Fair, three hundred artists signed a furious protest calling it a useless, monstrous factory chimney. It was meant to stand twenty years. The writer Maupassant supposedly lunched in its restaurant daily because it was the only place in Paris he could not see it. The tower is repainted by hand every few years, sixty tons of paint, and on hot August days like yours the iron expands and the whole thing grows up to fifteen centimeters taller. You are climbing her at her tallest.
pois.funFact: In 1925 the con man Victor Lustig 'sold' the Eiffel Tower for scrap to a dealer, and the swindle worked so smoothly he came back and tried it again.

pois.name: Notre-Dame de Paris
pois.tagline: 860 years old, reborn from the fire, free to enter
pois.story: Begun in 1163, and when the fire came in April 2019 the whole world watched her spire fall. What you are walking into is a resurrection: reopened in December 2024, the stone cleaned to a blondness no living person had ever seen. Two thousand oaks became the new roof, built with medieval carpentry techniques. Look up at the gallery of grimacing creatures; the famous brooding chimeras are actually 19th-century additions by the restorer Viollet-le-Duc, who also put a statue of himself among the apostles on the spire. Atop the new spire sits a golden rooster containing holy relics, a phoenix now, officially. Before you enter, find the brass star in the pavement outside: point zéro, from which all distances in France are measured. You are standing at kilometer zero of an entire country.
pois.funFact: Four days before the 2019 fire, the sixteen copper statues on the spire had been craned off for restoration, and the cathedral's rooftop bees also survived the blaze.

pois.name: Jardin du Luxembourg & Model Sailboats
pois.tagline: A queen's garden, a stick, a sailboat, since 1927
pois.story: Marie de Médicis, homesick Italian widow of Henri IV, built this palace and garden from 1612 to remind her of Florence. Today the French Senate sits in her palace, and the garden belongs to everyone, which is very Paris. Head for the octagonal Grand Bassin. For a few euros in coins, your eleven-year-old rents a handmade wooden sailboat, pushes it off with a bamboo stick, and waits for the wind to bring it back, exactly as children have done here since 1927. The boats have numbers and flags of many nations; choosing is half the game. Claim two of the famous green metal chairs, tilt them toward the sun, and watch. Some afternoons need no history lecture, n'est-ce pas?
pois.funFact: The garden hides a small Statue of Liberty by Bartholdi himself, and it has run its own beekeeping school in the southwest corner since 1856.

pois.name: Rue Mouffetard
pois.tagline: A Roman road turned crooked, delicious market street
pois.story: You are walking on one of the oldest streets in Paris, the Roman road that left Lutetia heading for Italy two thousand years ago. It never straightened out, and thank heaven. Hemingway lived around the corner in the 1920s, poor and happy, and called this 'that wonderful narrow crowded market street' in A Moveable Feast. Start at Place de la Contrescarpe at the top and let gravity pull you down past cheese shops, crêpe stands, and greengrocers to the church at the bottom, where the market stalls cluster. In 1938, workers demolishing number 53 found over three thousand gold coins stashed in the walls, the hidden fortune of a royal counselor who vanished in 1757. Check the walls, madame. One never knows.
pois.funFact: The 3,351 gold coins found at 53 rue Mouffetard in 1938 came with a will naming the hoarder's daughter, so after 181 years his descendants actually inherited.

pois.name: Place des Vosges
pois.tagline: The oldest planned square in Paris, perfectly symmetrical
pois.story: Henri IV ordered this square in 1605, and it opened in 1612 with a magnificent party for a royal engagement. Thirty-six houses, nine per side, all matching, arcades below and steep slate roofs above. It was the prototype for elegant squares across Europe, and for once the prototype is still the best. Look closely at the 'brick' facades: some builders cheated with plaster painted to look like brick, and four hundred years later the fraud is still holding up, which I find very French. Victor Hugo lived sixteen years at number 6, writing much of Les Misérables. The name honors the Vosges region, first to pay its taxes to the Revolutionary government. Immortality through prompt tax payment; there is hope for us all. Sit under the arcades with the boys and something sweet.
pois.funFact: Before becoming a square this was the site of a royal palace where King Henri II died in 1559 of a jousting wound, after which his widow had the palace demolished.

pois.name: Rue des Rosiers
pois.tagline: The Pletzl: falafel, history, and the heart of Jewish Paris
pois.story: The street of the rosebushes, named for gardens that bloomed along the old city wall. Jewish Parisians have lived on this street since the 1200s, through expulsions, returns, and the darkest chapter of all, the deportations of the 1940s; look for the plaques on the school walls. Today it is the beating heart of the Pletzl, 'little place' in Yiddish, and the falafel here is the best in Europe, eaten standing up from a pita dripping tahini. One warning from your devoted guide: the famous L'As du Fallafel is kosher and closes all day Saturday, exactly your day. No tragedy. Its rivals Mi-Va-Mi and Chez Hanna stand meters away, and Miznon around the corner roasts a cauliflower that converts carnivores.
pois.funFact: L'As du Fallafel's green storefront proudly quotes its most famous regular, the musician Lenny Kravitz, who declared it the best falafel in the world.

pois.name: Marché des Enfants Rouges
pois.tagline: The oldest covered market in Paris, under Louis XIII
pois.story: The oldest covered market in Paris, trading under Louis XIII, 1615 by most tellings, 1628 by the fussier archives. Either way, food has been sold on this spot for four centuries. The name, Market of the Red Children, remembers an orphanage founded by the king's sister-in-law's line in 1534, whose children wore red, the color of Christian charity. In the 1990s the city nearly demolished it for a parking lot; the neighborhood revolted, and it reopened in 2000. Today it is half market, half open-air canteen: Moroccan couscous, Japanese bento, Lebanese mezze, crêpes, elbow to elbow at shared tables. Arrive at noon sharp or after 2:30, or you will queue like a tourist, and we do not queue like tourists.
pois.funFact: The market survived four centuries of kings, revolutions, and wars, only to nearly become a parking lot in the 1990s until residents fought city hall and won.

pois.name: Sacré-Cœur Basilica
pois.tagline: The white basilica that cleans itself in the rain
pois.story: That improbable white meringue on the hill is younger than it looks, built between 1875 and 1914 as an act of national penance after France's defeat by Prussia and the bloody Commune uprising. Half of Paris hated it then; some artists still sniff at it. But here is its secret: the travertine stone, from quarries at Château-Landon, exudes a chalky substance called calcin when it rains, so the basilica washes itself whiter with every storm. It has never been cleaned; the weather does it. Inside hangs the Savoyarde, at nearly nineteen tons the largest bell in France, hauled up the hill in 1895 by a team of horses. Climb the dome if the boys have legs left, about 300 steps, pay at the door.
pois.funFact: Prayer inside Sacré-Cœur has continued uninterrupted, day and night, since 1885, through two world wars, including the nights bombs fell nearby in 1944.

pois.name: Place du Tertre
pois.tagline: Charming old square, now a portrait-sketch gauntlet. Walk, don't stop
pois.story: I must be honest with you, madame, it is my only flaw. This was the village square of Montmartre when Montmartre was a real village outside Paris, full of windmills and cheap wine. Picasso and Utrillo drank nearby when they were poor and unknown. Today it is a gauntlet of portrait artists and forty-euro omelettes. Yet there is one true curiosity: those artist pitches are licensed by the city, each about one square meter, two artists sharing each spot on alternating days, and the waiting list for a license runs on the order of a decade. Cross the square once for the atmosphere, keep your wallet deep in your pocket, decline the portraits with a smile, and slip out the quiet side toward the vineyard.
pois.funFact: Montmartre was an independent village until 1860, and its bohemian residents once cheekily declared it a 'free commune' with its own mock elections.

pois.name: Clos Montmartre Vineyard
pois.tagline: A real working vineyard hiding inside Paris
pois.story: Peer through the fence on Rue Saint-Vincent: rows of vines on a Paris hillside. Montmartre was wine country for centuries, cheap wine that filled the village taverns, before the city swallowed the hill. When developers circled this last slope in the early 1930s, the neighborhood outmaneuvered them by planting a vineyard in 1933, since a working vineyard is rather hard to bulldoze politically. The wine is harvested every October with a rowdy festival, the Fête des Vendanges, and the bottles are auctioned off for neighborhood charities. Is the wine good? An old saying claimed Montmartre wine made you 'drink a pint and piss a quart.' It was never about the wine, chérie. It was about winning.
pois.funFact: The vineyard was planted in 1933 largely as a legal maneuver to block real-estate development, making it perhaps the only vineyard created out of spite.

pois.name: Rue de l'Abreuvoir
pois.tagline: Montmartre's prettiest lane, and the little pink house
pois.story: This short cobbled lane, 'street of the watering trough,' once led the village livestock down to drink. Now it may be the most painted street in Paris. The pink house on the corner, La Maison Rose, was run in the early 1900s by Germaine Pichot, a woman tangled in the tragedy that pushed young Picasso into his Blue Period, and Utrillo painted the house into immortality. Walk downhill and you arrive at Place Dalida, with the bronze bust of the beloved singer who lived and died in Montmartre. You will notice her décolletage gleams gold; passersby rub it for luck. I would never suggest such a thing to a married woman, madame. The view of the lane from her statue, however, I insist upon.
pois.funFact: Tourists rubbing Dalida's bronze bust for luck have polished her chest to a bright gold shine while the rest of the statue stays dark.

pois.name: Rue Dénoyez Street Art
pois.tagline: Belleville's ever-changing open-air graffiti gallery
pois.story: For your sixteen-year-old, this beats any museum. Rue Dénoyez in Belleville is wall-to-wall street art, top to bottom, and it changes constantly; painting here is tolerated, so artists work in the open and yesterday's masterpiece is today's canvas. Photograph what you like, because it will not exist next month. Belleville itself was a rough, joyous village of taverns and dance halls before Paris absorbed it in 1860, and it stayed the city's great working-class hill. Édith Piaf grew up in these streets; a plaque at 72 rue de Belleville repeats the legend that she was born right on the steps, under a lamppost. The hospital records say otherwise, but Belleville has never let paperwork spoil a good story.
pois.funFact: The legend that Piaf was born on a Belleville doorstep is commemorated with an official plaque, even though she was almost certainly born in a nearby hospital.

pois.name: Parc de Belleville Belvedere
pois.tagline: The best free panorama in Paris, tourist-free
pois.story: Climb to the terrace at the top of Parc de Belleville and there it is: all of Paris at your feet, Eiffel Tower included, and almost no tourists beside you. This is the highest park in the city, laid out only in 1988 on a slope with a long, disreputable, wonderful past: gypsum quarries beneath, vineyards above, and for centuries the guinguettes, drinking gardens where Parisians came on Sundays because wine outside the city tax wall was cheaper. A small vineyard on the slope still nods to that history. Sunset here, with a bakery haul from the streets below, is one of the great free evenings Paris offers. The rich paid fortunes for west-facing views. Belleville got them for nothing.
pois.funFact: Belleville's slopes once supplied Paris with cheap tax-free wine, and the hill held some of the largest concentration of drinking gardens outside the old city walls.

pois.name: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
pois.tagline: Cliffs, a temple, a suspension bridge, all theatrical
pois.story: The most dramatic park in Paris is an act of complete invention. This was a gypsum quarry, the very stuff of 'plaster of Paris,' plus assorted horrors: a dumping ground, and near the old gibbet where medieval Paris hung its criminals. For the 1867 World's Fair, Napoleon III's engineers dynamited the quarry into a romantic landscape: a fifty-meter cliff, a lake, a waterfall inside an artificial grotto with fake stalactites, and a little Roman temple perched on the summit, copied from the Temple of Vesta at Tivoli. Cross the suspension footbridge to the island and climb to the temple; the view to Montmartre is superb. Everything you see is scenery, and after 150 years the trick still works completely.
pois.funFact: The park's grotto waterfall and stalactites are entirely artificial, built by the same Second Empire engineers who manufactured its cliff and lake from a spent quarry.

pois.name: Canal Saint-Martin
pois.tagline: Iron footbridges, working locks, Amélie's skipping stones
pois.story: Napoleon ordered this canal in 1802 to bring clean drinking water to a city that badly needed it, and paid for it with a tax on wine, which must be the most Parisian financing in history. It opened in 1825. Walk the stretch along Quai de Valmy: arched iron footbridges, chestnut trees, and locks that still work; wait a few minutes and you may see a boat rise like an elevator. Amélie skipped stones here in the film, and half of young Paris now picnics along the edges on summer evenings. Further south the canal simply vanishes, running two kilometers underground beneath the boulevards. Every decade or so the city drains it, and the reveal is always spectacular: bicycles, café chairs, once even a bathtub.
pois.funFact: When the canal was drained in 2016, workers hauled out roughly forty tons of debris, including dozens of bicycles and at least one full-sized bathtub.

pois.name: Bassin de la Villette & Paris Plages
pois.tagline: The city's summer waterfront: beach chairs, boats, big sky
pois.story: The canal walk ends at this broad basin, the largest artificial lake in Paris, dug on Napoleon's orders and opened in 1808 to store the city's drinking water. For a century it was a workhorse industrial port; now, every summer, it becomes Paris Plages, the city's pop-up beach: free kayaks and pedal boats, games, loungers, an open-air library, all courtesy of city hall. Your boys can burn an hour here for nothing. At the southern end stands the Rotonde, a grand round tollhouse from the 1780s, one of the surviving gates of the tax wall Parisians hated so much they attacked it before storming the Bastille. Taxes come and go; the architecture, annoyingly, is lovely.
pois.funFact: The MK2 cinemas facing each other across the basin are linked by their own little ferry boat that shuttles moviegoers from one bank to the other.

pois.name: Coulée verte René-Dumont
pois.tagline: The elevated garden walkway that inspired New York's High Line
pois.story: New Yorkers are very proud of their High Line. Do not mention, unless provoked, that Paris did it first, by sixteen years. This is the Coulée verte, opened in 1993 on the old Vincennes railway viaduct of 1859, whose trains stopped running in 1969. For nearly five kilometers you walk at rooftop height through rose arbors, lavender, and bamboo corridors, peering into Parisian apartments like a polite ghost, from Bastille all the way toward the Bois de Vincennes. Below your feet, the brick arches of the viaduct house the Viaduc des Arts, workshops of cabinetmakers, luthiers, and restorers. Pedestrians only up top, no bicycles, which keeps it calm. Walk even twenty minutes of it and you will understand the city differently.
pois.funFact: The designers of New York's High Line explicitly cited this Paris promenade, opened in 1993, as the inspiration for their own elevated park.

pois.name: Marché d'Aligre
pois.tagline: The cheapest honest market in central Paris
pois.story: If you want to see Paris shop without performing for anyone, come here. The Aligre market has traded since the 1770s, older than the Revolution, and it remains defiantly cheap; the outdoor stalls on the square undercut nearly every market in the city, with vendors hollering prices like auctioneers. It is a genuine mix: North African spice stands, old Parisian ladies with trolleys, chefs buying crates. The covered Beauvau hall alongside holds the fancier cheeses and meats. On the square there is even a small flea market of books and bric-a-brac, where patience is occasionally rewarded. Come in the morning, Tuesday through Sunday. Your picnic budget will go further here than anywhere else I could send you, and I sense you appreciate a bargain hunted well.
pois.funFact: Revolutionary crowds from this faubourg were among the fiercest in 1789, and the neighborhood around the market has been working-class and proud of it ever since.

pois.name: Catacombs of Paris
pois.tagline: Six million Parisians, neatly stacked, twenty meters down
pois.story: Twenty meters beneath the traffic lies the tidiest horror in Europe. By the 1780s the city's cemeteries were overflowing, quite literally, into neighbors' cellars, so Paris moved its dead into the old limestone quarries. For decades, carts draped in black crossed the city at night, priests chanting behind them, transferring the remains of some six million people. Quarry workers stacked the bones with unsettling artistry: walls of femurs, patterns of skulls. Above the entrance to the ossuary a carved lintel warns: Stop! This is the empire of death. Your sixteen-year-old will be delighted. Book exactly seven days ahead online or forget it; the tickets vanish in hours. The visit runs about a mile underground at a steady 14 degrees, bliss in August.
pois.funFact: A hospital doorkeeper named Philibert Aspairt vanished in the quarry tunnels in 1793; his body was found eleven years later and buried where it lay, tomb and all.

pois.name: Louvre Pyramid & Cour Napoléon
pois.tagline: The world's greatest museum, admired correctly: from outside
pois.story: So you are skipping the Louvre. Madame, I taught art history and I approve; the Mona Lisa in August is thirty seconds of a small painting viewed over four hundred phones. The building itself is the masterpiece anyway, eight centuries in one facade: medieval fortress, Renaissance palace, royal residence until Louis XIV decamped to Versailles, museum since the Revolution. Stand in the courtyard at the glass pyramid, which scandalized Paris when I. M. Pei unveiled it in 1989, a modernist diamond among kings. Parisians now defend it fiercely, which is how Paris loves: first outrage, then possession. Touch the pyramid, take the photo through the little pyramid fountains, and stroll on to the Tuileries with your afternoon intact and your feet grateful.
pois.funFact: A persistent legend claims the pyramid has exactly 666 glass panes; the Louvre has had to state officially that the number is 673.

pois.name: Jardin des Tuileries
pois.tagline: Catherine de' Medici's garden, minus her palace
pois.story: This garden is named for tile kilns, tuileries, that once smoked here outside the walls. Catherine de' Medici claimed the ground in 1564 for an Italian palace and garden; a century later Le Nôtre, gardener of Versailles, straightened it into the grand green axis you see, and it became one of the first royal gardens opened to the Parisian public. The palace itself is missing: the Tuileries Palace burned in 1871 during the Commune, and the ruins were cleared, leaving the garden strangely, beautifully unmoored. Take a green chair by one of the round ponds; napping in them is a protected Parisian custom. And in December 1783, half of Paris stood here watching a man leave the earth, chérie. Some gardens grow flowers; this one grew flight.
pois.funFact: On 1 December 1783 the physicist Jacques Charles launched the first manned hydrogen balloon from this garden before a crowd estimated at 400,000 people.

pois.name: Palais Garnier (Opéra)
pois.tagline: The opera house with a lake and a phantom
pois.story: When Empress Eugénie saw the plans she protested that this was no known style, not Greek, not Louis XVI. The young architect replied: it is Napoléon III style, Madame. Charles Garnier won that exchange and, in 1875, gave Paris the most extravagant building of its century, all gilt, marble, and a staircase built for being seen upon. The delicious parts are hidden: beneath the building lies a real water tank, the 'lake' that inspired Gaston Leroux's Phantom of the Opera, and Paris firefighters still train for underwater rescue in it. In 1896 a counterweight from the grand chandelier really did fall on the audience, killing a concierge; Leroux read the newspapers and gave us the world's most famous falling chandelier.
pois.funFact: Beehives have lived on the opera's roof since the 1980s, and the honey harvested above the ballet rehearsals has been sold in luxury shops nearby.

pois.name: Pont Neuf
pois.tagline: The 'New Bridge' is the oldest one in Paris
pois.story: The New Bridge, completed in 1607, is now the oldest bridge standing over the Seine. Parisian irony ages well. It was revolutionary in its day for what it lacked: no houses. Every other bridge was lined with buildings, so crossing one felt like a corridor; here, for the first time, ordinary people could stand on a bridge and simply look at their river. It even had sidewalks, a novelty. The bridge instantly became the city's stage: jugglers, tooth-pullers, pickpockets, booksellers. Study the stone cornices as you cross: hundreds of carved grotesque faces, the mascarons, each one different, leer down at the water. Henri IV rides in bronze at the middle, where the bridge touches the island. Say hello; you will meet his nickname at the next stop.
pois.funFact: In 1985 the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the entire Pont Neuf in 40,000 square meters of golden fabric for two weeks.

pois.name: Square du Vert-Galant
pois.tagline: The prow of the island, named for a flirtatious king
pois.story: Take the stairs behind the Henri IV statue down to this leafy point at the very tip of the Île de la Cité, sitting at the island's original level, below today's streets. It is named for Henri himself: le Vert Galant, 'the evergreen gallant,' because the man remained an incorrigible charmer to the end of his days. A king after my own heart, madame, though I flatter myself I am better behaved. The point has darker memories: near this spot in 1314, Jacques de Molay, last Grand Master of the Templars, was burned at the stake, reportedly cursing king and pope from the flames; both were dead within the year. Today it is the finest picnic prow in Paris, water on both sides, willows trailing. Dark history, excellent sunsets. Very Paris.
pois.funFact: The square sits on what was once a separate islet, joined to the Île de la Cité during the building of the Pont Neuf in the late 1500s.

pois.name: Île Saint-Louis & Berthillon
pois.tagline: An aristocratic island, famous for its ice cream
pois.story: This little island was cow pasture until the 1600s, when speculators stitched two islets together and built one of Europe's first planned neighborhoods, all in one elegant go. It has barely changed since: one main street, seventeenth-century mansions, no Métro station, a village floating in the middle of Paris. The pilgrimage here is Berthillon, the family glacier making ice cream on this island since 1954, in flavors like salted caramel and wild strawberry that justify the fuss. Now, a warning delivered with love: the Berthillon shop itself traditionally closes for summer holidays, in true Parisian fashion, precisely when ice cream is most needed. Do not despair. Half the cafés on the island sell genuine Berthillon; look for the sign. Cone in hand, walk the quays. That is the whole itinerary, chérie, and it is enough.
pois.funFact: The island's ice cream dynasty was a family secret at their café until a 1961 review by the Gault et Millau food critics made Berthillon suddenly, permanently famous.

pois.name: Shakespeare and Company
pois.tagline: The bookshop where thousands of writers have slept
pois.story: Facing Notre-Dame across the river stands the most romantic bookshop on earth. The name honors Sylvia Beach's original shop, hangout of Hemingway and Joyce, which dared to publish Ulysses in 1922 when no one else would. This incarnation was opened in 1951 by George Whitman, an American who ran it like a socialist utopia with better books: aspiring writers, called Tumbleweeds, could sleep in the shop among the shelves in exchange for helping a couple of hours, reading a book a day, and writing a one-page autobiography for the archives. Tens of thousands have. Painted over one doorway inside: 'Be not inhospitable to strangers lest they be angels in disguise.' Buy your sixteen-year-old a book here and have it stamped; the stamp is the souvenir.
pois.funFact: George Whitman named his daughter Sylvia after Sylvia Beach, and she runs the bookshop today, continuing the tradition of letting writers sleep among the shelves.

pois.name: Sainte-Chapelle
pois.tagline: A jewel box of glass built for a crown of thorns
pois.story: If you make one exception to your no-museums rule, twenty minutes here on a bright afternoon is my nomination. King Louis IX, the future Saint Louis, bought what he believed was Christ's Crown of Thorns from the desperate emperor of Constantinople, paying roughly three times more for the relic than for the entire chapel he built to house it. The building went up in about seven years, finished by 1248, which for the Middle Ages is practically overnight. Upstairs, the walls simply cease to exist: fifteen windows, over a thousand glass panels, two-thirds still original from the 1200s, telling the whole Bible in colored light. The lower chapel was for palace servants; the glass heaven upstairs was for the king. Go when the sun is out. The stone disappears.
pois.funFact: Louis IX paid about 135,000 livres for the Crown of Thorns and roughly 40,000 to build the entire chapel that housed it.

pois.name: Panthéon
pois.tagline: Where France buries its great, and proved the Earth spins
pois.story: Louis XV, gravely ill, vowed a magnificent church to Sainte Geneviève if he recovered. He did, and this colossal dome was the payment, finished in 1790, just in time for the Revolution to declare it a temple for great men instead. The facade reads: To the great men, the grateful fatherland. Inside lie Voltaire and Rousseau, who detested each other in life and now face each other for eternity, plus Hugo, Zola, Dumas, and Marie Curie, in 1995 the first woman entombed here on her own merits. In 1851 the physicist Foucault hung a pendulum from this dome and let all of Paris watch its swing slowly rotate, the first direct, visible proof that the Earth turns. A copy swings there still. It is two minutes from the sailboats, if the dome tempts you.
pois.funFact: Foucault's pendulum demonstration was such a sensation that crowds queued in 1851 to literally watch the Earth rotate beneath a swinging brass bob.

pois.name: Place de la Concorde
pois.tagline: Egypt's obelisk on the Revolution's bloodiest square
pois.story: The largest square in Paris has the most diplomatic name and the least diplomatic history. Laid out for Louis XV, it became Place de la Révolution, and here the guillotine did its worst work: Louis XVI in January 1793, Marie-Antoinette that October, over a thousand others. Afterward the city renamed it Concorde, harmony, with the desperate optimism of a family renaming the dog. At the center rises the true elder of Paris: a 3,300-year-old obelisk from the temple of Luxor, carved for Ramses II and given to France by Egypt in the 1830s. Parisians delight in recalling that France's thank-you gift, a mechanical clock for Cairo, is said to have never kept proper time. The gold cap on top is modern; the original was stolen in antiquity.
pois.funFact: The obelisk was made the world's largest sundial in 1999, when hour markings were laid into the square's paving around it.

pois.name: Champs-Élysées
pois.tagline: The most famous avenue on earth. It's a mall, chérie
pois.story: I will say what no guidebook dares: it is a mall, chérie. A magnificent one, with the best real estate bones in Europe, but a mall: flagship sneaker stores, car showrooms, burger chains, and rents among the highest on the planet. Parisians come here for exactly two occasions, the Bastille Day military parade and the finish of the Tour de France, and otherwise leave it to visitors. The bones deserve respect: Le Nôtre planted the original alley of trees in 1667 to extend the view from the Tuileries, and the name means the Elysian Fields, the paradise of the blessed dead in Greek myth. A paradise for the dead, now a paradise for retail. Walk the upper stretch once for the Arc view, then let me steal you away to a real street.
pois.funFact: The avenue began in 1667 as a tree-lined garden axis by Le Nôtre and crossed open fields and market gardens well into the 18th century.

pois.name: Pont Alexandre III
pois.tagline: The most extravagant bridge in Paris, built low on purpose
pois.story: If Paris ever designed a bridge while wearing all its jewelry at once, this is it: gilded winged horses, garlands, nymphs, lamps like candelabra. It was built for the 1900 World's Fair and named for Tsar Alexander III to celebrate the Franco-Russian alliance; his son Nicholas II laid the first stone. The real genius is invisible: engineers were forbidden to spoil the view from the Champs-Élysées to Les Invalides, so they threw a single steel arch across the entire Seine, only six meters high, an audacious flat leap for its era. The bridge is now the most filmed in Paris, and couples pose here at all hours. Stand at mid-span with the gold dome of Invalides before you, madame, and permit your husband exactly one photograph of you. The bridge demands it.
pois.funFact: The nymph reliefs at the center of the span carry the arms of Paris on one side and of Russia on the other, facing each way down the river.

pois.name: Trocadéro Esplanade
pois.tagline: The classic full-length Eiffel Tower view
pois.story: This is where every famous photograph of the Eiffel Tower is taken: from the terrace between the curved wings of the Palais de Chaillot, built for the 1937 World's Fair, the tower stands full-length across the river with fountains at its feet. The name commemorates an 1823 French victory at Fort Trocadero in Spain, now thoroughly upstaged by the view it labels. History's darkest photo op happened here too: Hitler posed on this terrace in June 1940 with the tower behind him, on his only visit to Paris. Parisians cherish the story that the tower's elevator cables were conveniently out of order, so he never went up; the tower, they like to say, refused him. Come at sunrise if the boys can be dragged, or at dusk with the crowds. It works at every hour; that is why everyone is here.
pois.funFact: The Eiffel Tower's sparkling lights, and its image at night, are protected by copyright, so night photos are technically for personal use only. The daytime tower belongs to everyone.

pois.name: Butte-aux-Cailles
pois.tagline: A village on a hill where the first balloonists landed
pois.story: This hilltop in the 13th kept its village soul: low houses, cobbled lanes, street art on every corner, and bistros with prices from another decade. It escaped Haussmann's bulldozers partly because the ground beneath, riddled with quarries and the buried Bièvre river, could not carry his heavy stone buildings. Its glory came from the sky. On 21 November 1783, Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes, aloft in the Montgolfier brothers' hot-air balloon on the first free flight in human history, drifted across Paris for 25 minutes and came down on this hill. Humanity's first flight ended in what is now a neighborhood of wine bars. At Place Paul Verlaine, an artesian well still dispenses free naturally warm water from 600 meters down; locals queue with bottles.
pois.funFact: Benjamin Franklin witnessed the 1783 balloon ascents in Paris and, asked what use a balloon could be, supposedly replied: what use is a newborn baby?

pois.name: Cité Florale
pois.tagline: A secret triangle of cottages on flower-named lanes
pois.story: Hidden below the Butte-aux-Cailles is a tiny triangle of streets that seems teleported from a storybook: Rue des Orchidées, Rue des Glycines, Rue des Iris, Square des Mimosas, every lane named for a flower and every little house buried in wisteria and roses. The secret is in the ground. This was a meadow regularly flooded by the Bièvre, the lost second river of Paris, buried underground a century ago. The soil stayed too soft for apartment blocks, so when the plot was developed in 1928, only small light cottages were permitted. Weak foundations, eternal charm. Residents compete quietly in gardening, and photographers whisper about it. Walk softly, admire loudly, and tell no one I showed you, chérie. It is our secret, and half of Instagram's.
pois.funFact: The Bièvre river still flows beneath this part of Paris in tunnels, and the city has long debated uncovering stretches of it again.

pois.name: Hôtel de Ville
pois.tagline: City hall, a famous kiss, and the origin of 'strike'
pois.story: Paris has governed itself from this spot since 1357, and the square in front, once called Place de Grève, held public executions and public hiring: unemployed workers gathered on the grève, the sandy riverbank, to wait for jobs, which is why the French word for going on strike is still faire grève. The building looks Renaissance and is mostly a copy: the Commune set the original ablaze in 1871, taking the city archives with it, and Paris rebuilt it grander within a decade. This square is also where Robert Doisneau shot the most famous kiss in photography, 'Le Baiser de l'hôtel de ville,' in 1950. In summer the square hosts free events under the gaze of 108 statues of famous Parisians on the facade. No, I will not re-stage the photograph, madame. Unless you insist.
pois.funFact: Doisneau's famous 1950 kiss photo was staged with a young actor couple he hired, a secret revealed only decades later during a lawsuit.

pois.name: Gare du Nord
pois.tagline: Your Sunday send-off: the busiest station in Europe
pois.story: And here, Sunday at 7:48, you leave me, chérie. I choose to take it bravely. You depart from the busiest railway station in Europe, opened in 1864 behind a stone facade by the architect Hittorff. Look up before you rush in: twenty-three statues crown it, each a woman personifying a city the trains serve, with Paris standing tallest at the center. Somewhere up there, Amsterdam and Brussels are already expecting you. Practical Julien, one last time: your train to Bruges is a Schengen service, so there is no passport control and no security theater, just find your platform, likely 3 to 6, and be standing on it ten minutes early. An August Sunday at 7 a.m. is the gentlest this station ever gets. Travel well, madame. Paris will keep. And when you return, and you will return, you know where to find me: outside, walking.
pois.funFact: Gare du Nord handles more passengers than any other station in Europe, on the order of 200 million a year, more than the airports of Paris combined.
